description: We are a multidisciplinary team of students from Poznan University of Technology, representing Automation and Robotics, Computer Science, and Artificial Intelligence. We combine strong technical backgrounds in AI, software development, and systems engineering to tackle complex challenges, turn bold ideas into working solutions, and build something awesome together!
summary:
Where on Earth would you test a lunar rover? We built Zodiak, an interactive atlas that helps mission teams shortlist field sites with terrain resembling candidate base regions near the Moon’s south pole.

details:
Zodiak is an interactive atlas for finding places on Earth whose terrain resembles terrain near the Moon’s south pole. A team preparing to test a rover can use it to find candidate areas, see which features they share with a lunar region, and decide where to look more closely.

How we find candidate sites?

We used NASA LOLA elevation data from seven candidate lunar base regions as our reference. We measured slopes, surface roughness, and closed depressions, then applied the same measurements to Copernicus elevation data on Earth. We analysed the terrain in cells about two kilometres wide, used ESA WorldCover to screen for ground cover, and grouped neighbouring cells with similar terrain into candidate patches. The default scan evaluated roughly 1.76 million cells and identified 3,175 candidate patches.

The way we defined exposed ground changed the results. When we included areas classified as moss and lichen, Siberia’s Putorana Plateau topped the ranking. When we kept only bare or sparsely vegetated ground, a site in Chile’s Atacama Desert came first. We kept both rankings in the atlas so users can see how that choice affects their search.

How teams use the atlas?

Users can choose a lunar region and decide what matters most for their search. A rover team might require gently sloping ground and give preference to larger areas of connected terrain. Each criterion can be ignored, included in the score, or required as a filter. Users can then explore candidates on a map, inspect their coordinates and measurements, and compare Earth and Moon terrain side by side in synchronized 3D views.

The result is a shortlist backed by measurements. A team can use it to decide which areas deserve a closer look and where to gather more detailed maps before a field visit.

What we checked?

In a separate check using the original lunar elevation grid, our calculated slopes differed from NASA’s published slope map by a median absolute difference of 0.042°. We also used NASA ICESat-2 laser profiles to check Earth slope estimates. A test against known analog sites performed close to chance at the map-tile scale, so we use the ranking to identify areas with comparable terrain measurements for further study.

We also compared two elevation maps of the same crater in Morasko, Poland. The finer map shows the rim clearly, while the survey map softens it. That example shows what the atlas can do at landscape scale and why a team would need finer maps to assess obstacles along a specific rover route.

Tools and development?

We built the data pipeline in Python, using Rasterio for elevation grids and NumPy and SciPy for terrain measurements and analysis. We developed on laptops and ran the large Earth scan on GitHub Actions. The atlas uses TypeScript, React, and Three.js and is hosted on Vercel. We provide the ranked results, data sources, and validation checks so others can trace a candidate back to the measurements and choices that put it on the map.
